summary: This standards-track document specifies conventions for using EdDSA with curve25519 and curve448 in the Cryptographic Message Syntax. EdDSA defines PureEdDSA and HashEdDSA modes, but HashEdDSA is not used with CMS.

eli5.summary: A way to sign messages with a modern signature method, with rules for how it fits inside secure message files.

subtitle: How to sign CMS messages with the modern Ed25519 and Ed448 signature algorithms.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needed agreed rules for carrying EdDSA signatures, including which hash to use and how to fill in each algorithm field.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC uses only PureEdDSA with Ed25519 and Ed448, no context string, and fixes the identifiers: SHA-512 for Ed25519 and SHAKE256 with a 512-bit output for Ed448.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can produce and check EdDSA-signed CMS data in a uniform way. HashEdDSA is deliberately left out because it offers no benefit when signed attributes are present.

today: RFC 8419 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2018. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
RFC 8419 sets out how to use the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA, defined in RFC 8032) with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 5652) signed-data content type. It covers two curves: EdDSA with curve25519 is called Ed25519, and EdDSA with curve448 is called Ed448.

For each curve, RFC 8032 defines two modes, PureEdDSA and HashEdDSA. This document uses only PureEdDSA, and no context string is used with CMS.
sections.eli5: Imagine a standard way to sign a letter with a special pen. This document says how to use two versions of that pen on secure digital messages.

sections.title: EdDSA and Why Only the Pure Mode
sections.content:
EdDSA is a variant of Schnorr's signature system with (possibly twisted) Edwards curves. Ed25519 is intended to operate at around the 128-bit security level, and Ed448 at around the 224-bit security level.

One EdDSA parameter is the prehash function. If it is the identity function, the result is called PureEdDSA. If it is a collision-resistant hash function, the result is HashEdDSA. In most situations a CMS SignedData already carries signed attributes that include a message digest of the content. Because HashEdDSA offers no benefit when signed attributes are present, only PureEdDSA is used with CMS.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to prepare a letter before signing it. Since the letter already comes with a summary card attached, the extra preparing step would be a waste, so only the simple way is used.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Signature Values
sections.content:
Each algorithm is named by an object identifier. The EdDSA identifiers come from RFC 8410 and are repeated here: id-Ed25519 is 1 3 101 112 and id-Ed448 is 1 3 101 113. They identify public keys in certificates and are also used for signature values. When they identify a signature algorithm, the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be absent.

The data to be signed is processed with PureEdDSA, then a private key operation produces the signature value. As in RFC 8032, that value is the opaque string ENC(R) || ENC(S). It is encoded as an ASN.1 OCTET STRING and placed in the signature field of SignerInfo.
sections.eli5: Every kind of signature has a number name so computers can tell them apart. The signature itself is just a long string of bytes put in the right box on the form.

sections.title: Signed-data With and Without Signed Attributes
sections.content:
Including signed attributes is preferred, and the no-attributes form is given for completeness. With signed attributes, the message digest is computed over the eContent value. For Ed25519 the digest algorithm MUST be SHA-512, and for Ed448 it MUST be SHAKE256 with a 512-bit output. In SignerInfo, Ed25519 uses id-sha512 with absent parameters, while Ed448 uses id-shake256-len with the parameter present and containing 512 as a positive integer. The message-digest attribute MUST be included and must hold that digest.

Without signed attributes, the rules are simpler. Ed25519 uses id-sha512 and Ed448 uses id-shake256, both with absent parameters. The RFC notes that these hashes are used as part of the signing operation, but the signing operation does not take a digest computed with them as input.

In both forms the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm MUST be id-Ed25519 or id-Ed448 with absent parameters, and the signature field holds the octet string from the EdDSA private key signing operation.
sections.eli5: The best way is to attach a short summary of the letter before signing. There is also a way to skip the summary, but it is only there so the rulebook is complete.

sections.title: Implementation Warning: Two Passes
sections.content:
The RFC repeats a warning from RFC 8032: PureEdDSA requires two passes over the input. Many existing APIs, protocols and environments assume signature algorithms need only one pass, and may have API or bandwidth concerns supporting anything else.

This matters most when signed-data is used without signed attributes and the content to be signed might be quite large.
sections.eli5: To sign, the pen has to read the whole letter twice. That is awkward if the letter is huge and you can only look at it once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must protect the EdDSA private key, since compromise may allow forged signatures. Key generation relies on random numbers, and a poor pseudo-random number generator can leave little or no security. The RFC points to RFC 4086 for guidance on quality randomness.

Unlike DSA and ECDSA, EdDSA does not need a random value for each signature operation. The same private key SHOULD NOT be used with more than one set of EdDSA parameters, although there appear to be no security concerns when using the same key with PureEdDSA and HashEdDSA. Finally, the same hash function SHOULD be used for all operations when computing signatures, which reduces the number of failure points.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Keep your signing pen locked up, and make its secret pattern truly random. Do not use one pen for different signing styles.
